posts.title: The Art of Releasing Resentment in Your ADHD Relationship
posts.description: Resentment – the anger, bitterness, and disappointment that build from the feeling we’ve been wronged and treated unfairly over time – is a slowly simmering emotion. Eventually, its toxic burn clouds the way we view our relationship and may even suffocate it. In relationships touched by ADHD, traits like forgetfulness , disorganization, and inconsistent follow-through can hasten these feelings and chip away at intimacy. ADHD partners, in turn, commonly resent their neurotypical partners for misunderstanding the condition and setting unrealistic expectations. Resentment is a protective, multilayered emotion that deserves reflection. Follow these steps to gradually untangle the complex feelings you may be harboring about your partner so you can let go of resentment and start healing. posts.title: What Wears You Out at Social Gatherings? Take This Quiz
posts.description: We know that social gatherings are opportunities for bonding and connection. At the same time, they can leave ADHD brains feeling wiped out. From sensory overload and masking to unsolicited comments about neurodivergence, social and family gatherings can be draining, which is why it’s important to know yourself, plan ahead, take breaks, and build in recovery time. This self-test can help you identify where your energy goes and what might make your next gathering easier. Think about the social or holiday gatherings you've attended, hosted, or helped plan recently. How much did each of the following wear you out? Hearing someone dismiss ADHD or another aspect of my/my loved one's neurodivergence. posts.title: Scaling the Wall of Awful
posts.description: Here’s a familiar scenario: Your student with ADHD sits at the kitchen table, supposedly doing homework. Twenty minutes go by, and you check on their status. Nothing has been accomplished. In these moments, your child is invisibly, involuntarily grappling with the Wall of Awful , a term I coined to describe the emotional barrier people confront when faced with draining and/or daunting tasks (homework is a good example). Before your child can engage in work, they must get past this wall of emotions. The Wall of Awful Is Not Defiance Many parents misinterpret the early warning signs of the Wall. They mistake difficulty starting a task for resistance or defiance. So they double down on being a taskmaster, or, alternatively, they hover and provide too much help. Neither tactic aids their child in the long run.
